messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Matthias is a 52-year-old film director who came to treatment months after a life-threatening accident on location that still feels to him less like something that happened in the past than something waiting just off camera. During a night shoot in a remote industrial area, a lighting rig failed and crashed as a vehicle was being repositioned. In the confusion that followed, power dropped out across part of the set, leaving stretches of sudden darkness broken by harsh work lights, shouted instructions, and the metallic blast of equipment hitting concrete. Matthias was knocked down and briefly trapped amid cables and debris, convinced for several seconds that another collapse was coming and that he might die before anyone reached him. What remains with him now is not a coherent story but a sequence of sharp images: the angled glare of a work lamp, sparks, the black gap beyond the set, a twisted stand descending into view. He says the memory is extraordinarily clear and detailed, yet when he tries to describe it aloud he loses his words and becomes frustrated, as if the event exists in pictures his mind can replay but not translate.

That quality of memory has worn on his sense of himself. Because the accident returns in these vivid, mostly visual fragments that he cannot fully put into language, Matthias has come to believe there is something fundamentally inadequate about him. He compares his current state to the composed, decisive director he had always known himself to be and thinks, with shame, that his reactions prove he is a lousy coper. At times he says he barely recognizes the man he has become: someone derailed by a moment on his own set, unable even to give a straightforward account of it.

Those conclusions have shaped how he lives day to day. Convinced that his ongoing reactions mean weakness rather than injury, he works hard to manage them privately. He distracts himself relentlessly, burying himself in editing notes, streaming rough cuts late into the night, or scrolling through production schedules whenever his mind drifts toward the accident. He also finds himself circling the same unanswerable question—why this happened to him, why on a set he was responsible for, why he was the one who cannot seem to move on. Most concretely, he avoids circumstances that remind him of that night, especially darkness. He has started insisting on overlit rooms at home and on set, delegating night exterior shoots when he can, lingering in his trailer until others have checked locations first. The more he sees these maneuvers as necessary, the more they seem to confirm his view that he is no longer capable in the way he once was.

At work, the sensory world of filmmaking has become a minefield. Unexpected bangs from dropped equipment, a slammed stage door, or a sound cue played too loudly can make him jolt violently. He scans constantly for what might go wrong, listening for changes in the room and tracking crew movement with a vigilance he did not have before. Those reactions are tied not only to the set environment but to the way the accident lives in his mind: a sudden metallic crash or the hum-and-cut of power can call up the image of the rig falling so quickly that his body responds before he has fully registered where he is. Once that happens, he becomes even more watchful, certain that if he lets his guard down he will be caught off balance again.

That sense of threat feeds directly into further avoidance. If a sound check is chaotic or a generator backfires, Matthias may abruptly step away under the pretense of taking a call, then remain in brighter, quieter areas for the rest of the shift. He tells himself he is being practical, but his world has narrowed. Crew members have noticed he is less available during complicated setups, and his partner has noticed that he keeps lamps on throughout the apartment and changes the subject when the accident comes up. His attempts to distract himself and stay away from reminders have not softened the memory. If anything, the images intrude more forcefully in the spaces he is trying to outrun, and because he never stays with them long enough to make them into a fuller narrative, they remain jagged, sensory, and immediate.

Over time this pattern has tightened. The more Matthias avoids darkness, distracts himself, and searches for a reason the accident happened, the more fragile and altered he feels; the more fragile he feels, the more he monitors for danger and braces at ordinary sounds. He finally sought help after startling so badly at a crashing prop case during a daytime production meeting that he knocked over his chair in front of his crew. What frightened him most was not just the embarrassment, but the thought that this was who he is now—someone unrecognizable to himself, always on guard, ruled by images he cannot master. What he hopes, cautiously, is that he can find a way to speak about the accident without being swallowed by it, and return to a set without feeling that catastrophe is about to happen again.
